'''Susan Adele Greenfield, Baroness Greenfield''', {{postnominals|country=GBR|size=100%|sep=,|CBE|FRCP}}<ref name="baroness">{{cite web|url=https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/ld200102/minutes/010626/ldminute.htm|title=Minutes and Order Paper – Minutes of Proceedings|access-date=27 October 2007|publisher=UK Parliament House of Lords|year=2001|author=House of Lords}}</ref> (born 1 October 1950) is an English scientist, writer, broadcaster and member of the [[House of Lords]] (since 2001). Her research has focused on the treatment of [[Parkinson's disease]] and [[Alzheimer's disease]]. She is also interested in the [[neuroscience]] of [[consciousness]]<ref>[http://www.susangreenfield.com/about-susan/books#The Private Life of the Brain (2000)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180930030414/http://www.susangreenfield.com/about-susan/books#The |date=30 September 2018 }}, susangreenfield.com; accessed 5 April 2016.</ref> and the impact of technology on the brain.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Screen Technologies|url=http://www.susangreenfield.com/science/screen-technologies|website=susangreenfield.com|access-date=17 September 2015|archive-date=27 August 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190827063716/http://www.susangreenfield.com/science/screen-technologies/}}</ref>

Greenfield is a senior research fellow at [[Lincoln College, Oxford University|Lincoln College, Oxford]];<ref name="pharma">[http://www.pharm.ox.ac.uk/research/associate/susan-greenfield University of Oxford> Department of Pharmacology> Baroness Susan Greenfield] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140812080638/http://www.pharm.ox.ac.uk/research/associate/susan-greenfield |date=12 August 2014 }} Accessed 12 June 2015.</ref> she was a professor of [[Synaptic Pharmacology]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Susan Greenfield — Department of Physiology, Anatomy and Genetics (DPAG) |url=https://www.dpag.ox.ac.uk/women-in-physiology-anatomy-genetics/susan-greenfield |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20260411073458/https://www.dpag.ox.ac.uk/women-in-physiology-anatomy-genetics/susan-greenfield |archive-date=2026-04-11 |access-date=2026-11-11 |website=www.dpag.ox.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref>

Greenfield was chancellor of [[Heriot-Watt University]] in Edinburgh between 2005 and 2013.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Greenfield to be made Heriot-Watt chancellor|url=https://www.theguardian.com/education/2006/jan/31/highereducation.careers|newspaper=The Guardian|access-date=5 April 2016|first=Liz|last=Ford|date=31 January 2006 }}</ref> From 1998 to 2010, she was director of the [[Royal Institution of Great Britain]].<ref name="times">{{cite news|url=http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/news/science/article6981622.ece|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100603093947/http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/news/science/article6981622.ece|archive-date=3 June 2010|title=Baroness Greenfield loses her job in Royal Institution shake-up|access-date=9 January 2010|newspaper=The Times|author=The Times|location=London, UK|date=9 January 2010}}</ref> In September 2013, she co-founded the biotech company Neuro-bio Ltd, where she is chief executive officer.

==Early life==

Greenfield's mother, Doris (née Thorp), was a dancer and a Christian, and her father, Reginald Myer Greenfield, was an electrician who was the son of a Yiddish-speaking Jewish immigrant from Austria; her grandmothers never spoke to each other and she said of them, "the prejudice was equally vociferous on both sides".<ref>{{cite news|last1=Franks|first1=Lynne|title=Interview: Susan Greenfield|url=https://www.thejc.com/life/interview-susan-greenfield-jza3hudo|work=The Jewish Chronicle|date=24 November 2011}}</ref><ref name=guardian2004>{{cite news|last=Radford|first=Tim|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2004/apr/30/science.highereducation|title=The Guardian profile: Susan Greenfield|newspaper=The Guardian|date=30 April 2004|access-date=26 August 2011|location=London, UK}}</ref>

==Education==

She attended the [[Godolphin and Latymer School]], where she took [[A level]]s in Latin, Greek and ancient history, and maths. The first member of her immediate family to go to university, she was initially admitted to [[St Hilda's College, Oxford|St Hilda's College]] to read Philosophy and Psychology, but changed course and graduated with a first-class degree in experimental psychology.<ref name=guardian2004/><ref>{{cite news|last1=Bell|first1=Matthew|title=Susan Greenfield: After the science, the fiction|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/profiles/susan-greenfield-after-the-science-the-fiction-8679982.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220525/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/profiles/susan-greenfield-after-the-science-the-fiction-8679982.html |archive-date=25 May 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|work=The Independent on Sunday|date=30 June 2013}}</ref> As a Senior Scholar at [[St Hugh's College, Oxford]],<ref name="bc">{{cite web|url=http://www.britishcouncil.org/science-testimonials-baroness-greenfield.htm|title=Baroness Greenfield|access-date=27 October 2007|publisher=British Council on Science|year=2007|author=British Council on Science|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070828023257/http://www.britishcouncil.org/science-testimonials-baroness-greenfield.htm|archive-date=28 August 2007}}</ref> she completed her [[Doctor of Philosophy|DPhil]] degree in 1977 under the supervision of [[A. David Smith|Anthony David Smith]] on the ''Origins of [[acetylcholinesterase]] in [[cerebrospinal fluid]]''.<ref name="greenfieldphd">{{cite thesis|degree=DPhil|first=Susan|last=Greenfield|title=Origins of acetylcholinesterase in cerebrospinal fluid|publisher=University of Oxford|date=1977|url=http://solo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/primo_library/libweb/action/display.do?doc=oxfaleph016961302|archive-date=16 November 2018|access-date=12 September 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181116043213/http://solo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/primo_library/libweb/action/display.do?doc=oxfaleph016961302}}</ref>

She then held a junior research fellowship at Green College, Oxford between 1981 and 1984.<ref>{{Cite news|title=The Guardian profile: Susan Greenfield|url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2004/apr/30/science.highereducation|newspaper=The Guardian|access-date=17 September 2015|first=Tim|last=Radford|date=30 April 2004 }}</ref>

==Career==
[[File:Baroness Susan Greenfield Pierhead Session crop.jpg|thumb|left|Greenfield at [[Senedd Cymru – Welsh Parliament]]; 2013]]

Greenfield's research is focused on brain physiology, particularly on the brain mechanisms of [[Parkinson's disease|Parkinson's]] and [[Alzheimer's disease|Alzheimer's]] diseases. She is also known for her role in popularising science. Greenfield has written several books about the brain, regularly gives public lectures, and appears on radio and television.<ref>{{IMDb name|1799870}}</ref>

Since 1976, Greenfield has published approximately 200 papers in [[Academic journal|peer-reviewed journals]], including studies on brain mechanisms involved in addiction and reward,<ref name=functionaldomains>{{Cite journal|pmid=12097522|pmc=6758186|year=2002|last1=Cragg|first1=S.J.|title=Functional domains in dorsal striatum of the nonhuman primate are defined by the dynamic behavior of dopamine|journal=The Journal of Neuroscience|volume=22|issue=13|pages=5705–12|last2=Hille|first2=C. J.|last3=Greenfield|first3=S.A.|doi=10.1523/JNEUROSCI.22-13-05705.2002}}</ref><ref name="dopaminerelease">{{Cite journal|pmid=11050144|pmc=6772736|year=2000|last1=Cragg|first1=S.J.|title=Dopamine release and uptake dynamics within nonhuman primate striatum in vitro|journal=The Journal of Neuroscience|volume=20|issue=21|pages=8209–17|last2=Hille|first2=C.J.|last3=Greenfield|first3=S.A.|doi=10.1523/JNEUROSCI.20-21-08209.2000}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|doi=10.1006/exnr.2000.7420|pmid=10877925|title=Real-Time Dynamics of Dopamine Released from Neuronal Transplants in Experimental Parkinson's Disease|journal=Experimental Neurology|volume=164|issue=1|pages=145–53|year=2000|last1=Cragg|first1=S.J.|last2=Clarke|first2=D.J.|last3=Greenfield|first3=S.A.|s2cid=20654732}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|pmid=9539208|year=1998|last1=Cragg|first1=S.J.|title=Dopamine is released spontaneously from developing midbrain neurons in organotypic culture|journal=Neuroscience|volume=84|issue=2|pages=325–30|last2=Holmes|first2=C.|last3=Hawkey|first3=C.R.|last4=Greenfield|first4=S.A.|doi=10.1016/s0306-4522(97)00657-x|s2cid=25909469}}</ref><ref name=neurotoxic>{{Cite journal|pmid=9157319|year=1996|last1=Dickie|first1=B. G.|title=Neurotoxic and neurotrophic effects of chronic N-methyl-D-aspartate exposure upon mesencephalic dopaminergic neurons in organotypic culture|journal=Neuroscience|volume=72|issue=3|pages=731–41|last2=Holmes|first2=C.|last3=Greenfield|first3=S.A.|doi=10.1016/0306-4522(95)00611-7|s2cid=23225163}}</ref> relating to [[dopamine]] systems and other neurochemicals.<ref>{{Cite journal|doi=10.1016/j.neuroscience.2009.10.005|pmid=19819310|title=5-HT1B receptor regulation of serotonin (5-HT) release by endogenous 5-HT in the substantia nigra|journal=Neuroscience|volume=165|issue=1|pages=212–20|year=2010|last1=Threlfell|first1=S.|last2=Greenfield|first2=S. A.|last3=Cragg|first3=S.J.|s2cid=25730390}}</ref><ref name="doi10.1111/j.1471-4159.2008.05646.x|noedit">{{Cite journal|doi=10.1111/j.1471-4159.2008.05646.x|pmid=18761715|title=Constitutive histamine H2receptor activity regulates serotonin release in the substantia nigra|journal=Journal of Neurochemistry|volume=107|issue=3|pages=745–55|year=2008|last1=Threlfell|first1=S.|last2=Exley|first2=R.|last3=Cragg|first3=S. J.|last4=Greenfield|first4=S. A.|s2cid=39736774|doi-access=}}</ref> She investigated the brain mechanisms underlying [[attention deficit hyperactivity disorder]] ([[ADHD]])<ref name="doi10.1111/j.1471-4159.2008.05646.x|noedit"/><ref>{{Cite journal|doi=10.1101/Lm.1092608|title=Methylphenidate amplifies long-term plasticity in the hippocampus via noradrenergic mechanisms|journal=Learning & Memory|volume=15|issue=8|pages=580–86|year=2008|last1=Dommett| first1=E.J.|last2=Henderson|first2=E. L.|last3=Westwell|first3=M. S.|last4=Greenfield|first4=S.A.|pmid=18685149|doi-access=free}}</ref> as well as the impact of [[environmental enrichment]].<ref>{{Cite journal|doi=10.1016/j.neuroscience.2010.07.029|pmid=20654700|title=Environmental enrichment differentially modifies specific components of sensory-evoked activity in rat barrel cortex as revealed by simultaneous electrophysiological recordings and optical imaging in vivo|journal=Neuroscience|volume=170|issue=2|pages=662–69|year=2010|last1=Devonshire |first1=I. M.|last2=Dommett|first2=E. J.|last3=Grandy|first3=T. H.|last4=Halliday|first4=A. C.|last5=Greenfield|first5=S. A.|s2cid=23618724}}</ref>

In 1994, she was the first woman to give the [[Royal Institution Christmas Lectures]], then sponsored by the [[BBC]]. Her lectures were titled "Journey to the centre of the brain".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rigb.org/assets/uploads/docs/ListofLecturers.pdf|title=List of Lecturers|access-date=9 January 2010|publisher=RI|author=RI|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100617044333/http://www.rigb.org/assets/uploads/docs/ListofLecturers.pdf|archive-date=17 June 2010}}</ref> She was appointed Director of the [[Royal Institution]] in 1998.<ref>[http://www.rigb.org/contentControl?action=displayContent&id=00000001885 Profile] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721185206/http://www.rigb.org/contentControl?action=displayContent&id=00000001885 |date=21 July 2011 }}, rigb.org; accessed 5 April 2016.</ref> The post was abolished in 2010.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/science/science-news/6968961/Baroness-Greenfields-redundancy-only-way-to-get-rid-of-her.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100113194432/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/science/science-news/6968961/Baroness-Greenfields-redundancy-only-way-to-get-rid-of-her.html|archive-date=13 January 2010|location=London, UK|work=The Daily Telegraph|first1=Caroline|last1=Gammell|first2=Richard|last2=Alleyne|title=Baroness Greenfield's redundancy 'only way to get rid of her'|date=12 January 2010}}</ref> The Royal Institution had found itself in a financial crisis following a £22m development programme led by Greenfield and the board. The project ended £3 million in debt.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/science/science-news/6968961/Baroness-Greenfields-redundancy-only-way-to-get-rid-of-her.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100113194432/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/science/science-news/6968961/Baroness-Greenfields-redundancy-only-way-to-get-rid-of-her.html|archive-date=13 January 2010|title=Baroness Greenfield's redundancy 'only way to get rid of her'|newspaper=Telegraph|access-date=28 April 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=Robin McKie and Rajeev Syal|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2010/jan/10/greenfield-redundancy-royal-institution|title=Top scientist Susan Greenfield told to quit her job – and her flat|newspaper=The Observer |date=10 January 2010 |publisher=Theguardian.com|access-date=28 April 2014}}</ref> Greenfield subsequently announced that she would be taking her employers to an employment tribunal and her claim would include discrimination.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/sci/tech/8449718.stm|title=Royal Institution former chief suing for discrimination|access-date=9 January 2010|publisher=BBC|author=BBC|date=9 January 2010}}</ref> The case was settled out of court.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.civilsociety.co.uk/governance/news/content/6560/baroness_greenfield_drops_sex_discrimination_case_against_the_royal_institution|title=Baroness Greenfield drops legal action against the Royal Institution|publisher=Civilsociety.co.uk|access-date=28 April 2014}}</ref>

Greenfield's two main positions at Oxford were Tutorial Fellow in Medicine at Lincoln College Oxford,<ref name="pharma"/> and Professor of Synaptic Pharmacology.{{citation needed|date=June 2015}} Between 1995 and 1999, she gave public lectures as [[Gresham Professor of Physic]] in London. Greenfield was [[Adelaide]]'s [[Thinker in Residence]] for 2004 and 2005.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thinkers.sa.gov.au/thinkers/Greenfield/|title=Adelaide Thinkers in Residence – Susan Greenfield|publisher=Govt. of South Australia|access-date=3 March 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110222003150/http://thinkers.sa.gov.au/thinkers/greenfield/|archive-date=22 February 2011}}</ref>

As a result of her recommendations,{{citation needed|date=April 2016}} South Australian Premier Mike Rann made a major funding commitment, backed by the state and federal governments and the private sector, to establish the [[Royal Institution of Australia]] and the Australian Science Media Centre in Adelaide.<ref>[http://www.adelaidenow.com.au/news/south-australia/m-to-form-royal-institution-of-australia/story-e6frea83-1225712522600 $15m to form Royal Institution of Australia] ''The Advertiser'', 15 May 2009; accessed 10 September 2014.</ref>

She has explored the relevance of neuroscience knowledge to education<ref name="doi10.1177/1073858409356111|noedit">{{Cite journal|doi=10.1177/1073858409356111|pmid=20484219|title=From Scientific Theory to Classroom Practice|journal=The Neuroscientist|volume=17|issue=4| pages=382–88|year=2010|last1=Dommett|first1=E.J.|last2=Devonshire|first2=I.M.|last3=Plateau|first3=C.R.|last4=Westwell|first4=M.S.|last5=Greenfield|first5=S. A.|s2cid=38863068}}</ref> and has used the phrase "mind change",<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/video/2011/aug/15/susan-greenfield-video|title=Susan Greenfield: "Mind change is 'an issue that's as important and as unprecedented as climate change"|newspaper=Guardian|access-date=17 June 2013|location=London|first1=Mustafa|last1=Khalili|first2=Elliot|last2=Smith|first3=Philip|last3=Oltermann|date=15 August 2011}}</ref> an umbrella term comparable to "climate change", encompassing diverse issues involved in the impact of the 21st-century environment on the brain.<ref>{{cite book|last=Greenfield|first=Susan|url=http://www.nottinghilleditions.com/books/you-and-me-the-neuroscience-of-identity/170|title=You And Me: The Neuroscience of Identity|publisher=Notting Hill Editions|access-date=17 June 2013|archive-date=24 April 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130424203711/http://www.nottinghilleditions.com/books/you-and-me-the-neuroscience-of-identity/170}}</ref>

In 2013 she co-founded the biotech company Neuro-Bio Ltd which develops diagnostic tests and therapeutics for [[Alzheimer's disease]]. The company has found that the [[C terminus]] of [[acetylcholinesterase]] can be cleaved and that the resulting peptide can kill neurons; the company has also found that a [[cyclic peptide]] analogue could prevent that neuronal death.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Koch|first1=Selina|last2=Zipkin|first2=Mark|title=Why Neuro-Bio thinks it's time to revisit the role of AChE in AD|url=https://www.biocentury.com/bc-innovations/targets-mechanisms/2016-06-30/why-neuro-bio-thinks-its-time-revisit-role-ache-ad?kwh=Neuro-Bio|work=BioCentury|date=30 June 2016}}</ref> The company raised around $4 million in 2017.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Ross|first1=John|title=Commercialising research: the deal as learning curve|url=https://www.theaustralian.com.au/higher-education/commercialising-research-the-deal-as-learning-curve/news-story/eadc9f81ffa3b5bbef993c2efd37e10c|work=The Australian|url-access=subscription|date=17 March 2017}}</ref>

==Politics==
[[File:Susan Greenfield 2013b.jpg|thumb|Greenfield in 2013]]
Greenfield sits in the [[Parliament of the United Kingdom]] in the [[House of Lords]] as a [[crossbencher]], having no formal political affiliation.<ref>{{cite web|title=Baroness Greenfield|work=UK Parliament website |url=http://www.parliament.uk/biographies/susan-greenfield/27126|access-date=19 July 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100612081431/http://www.parliament.uk/biographies/susan-greenfield/27126|archive-date=12 June 2010}}</ref> Records of Greenfield's activity in the House of Lords indicate abstention on a range of issues.<ref>{{cite web|title=Baroness Greenfield profile at|work=TheyWorkForYou|publisher=mySociety|url=https://www.theyworkforyou.com/peer/baroness_greenfield#votingrecord|access-date=19 July 2010}}</ref> She has spoken on a variety of topics,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Baroness Susan Greenfield; House of Lords debates|url=http://www.susangreenfield.com/public-speaking/house-of-lords-debates|website=www.susangreenfield.com|access-date=18 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151215082218/http://www.susangreenfield.com/public-speaking/house-of-lords-debates/|archive-date=15 December 2015}}</ref> including education, drugs, and economic empowerment for women.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Lords Hansard text for 05 Mar 2015 (pt 0001)|url=https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/ld201415/ldhansrd/text/150305-0001.htm#15030536000274|website=www.publications.parliament.uk|access-date=17 September 2015}}</ref>

==Books==

In 2013, Greenfield published a dystopian [[science-fiction]] novel, ''2121: A Tale from the Next Century'', telling the story of videogame-playing hedonists and their conflict with "Neo-Puritans".<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.oxfordtimes.co.uk/news/features/10603109.Susan_Greenfield__Tale_of_a_terrible_reckoning/|title=Susan Greenfield: Tale of a terrible reckoning|first=Reg|last=Little|newspaper=[[Oxford Times]]|date=9 August 2013}}</ref>

In 2014, Greenfield published a [[popular science]] book called ''Mind Change: How Digital Technologies are Leaving their Mark on our Brains,'' describing her ideas about [[#Impact of digital technology controversy|the impact of digital technology]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Robbins|first1=Martin|title=Mind Change: Susan Greenfield has a Big Idea, but What is it?|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/the-lay-scientist/2014/oct/03/mind-change-susan-greenfield-has-a-big-idea-but-what-is-it|access-date=6 October 2017|agency=The Guardian}}</ref>

==Impact of digital technology controversy==
{{Anchor|Controversy}}
Greenfield has expressed concerns that internet usage may modify the brain structures of youngsters.<ref>{{cite episode|title=Social websites: bad for kids' brains?|series=BBC Newsnight|series-link=Newsnight|airdate=25 February 2009|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/programmes/newsnight/7909847.stm|access-date=6 January 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/blog/2009/feb/25/social-networking|title=Age Concern backs social networks but Ben Goldacre's blood pressure still rising|last=Arthur|first=Charles|date=25 February 2009|work=guardian.co.uk|access-date=14 March 2009|location=London, UK}}</ref>

She has had controversy surrounding her opinions on the relationship between technology use and [[Autism Spectrum Disorder]]. She originally linked the increase in Autism Spectrum Disorder diagnosis to increased screen-time in a 2011 [[New Scientist]] article,.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg21128236-400-susan-greenfield-living-online-is-changing-our-brains/ | title=Susan Greenfield: Living online is changing our brains }}</ref> She defended this claim in 2014, in an interview with [[Stephen Sackur]], on the BBC show [[HARDTalk]], in which she claims to have collated 500 articles "in support of the possible problematic effects" of technology-use.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b04j6gl1 | title=BBC News Channel – HARDtalk, Professor Susan Greenfield – Neuroscientist }}</ref>

She noted that [[Public Health England]] had related social networking and multiplayer online games to "lower levels of wellbeing", and believed that evidence pointed to a "[[dose–response relationship|dose response]]" relationship, "where each additional hour of viewing increases the likelihood of experiencing socio-emotional problems".<ref>{{Cite web|title=Main heading|url=http://data.parliament.uk/writtenevidence/committeeevidence.svc/evidencedocument/health-committee/childrens-and-adolescent-mental-health-and-camhs/written/7562.html|website=data.parliament.uk|access-date=18 September 2015}}</ref> She believed this raised questions about where to draw the boundaries between beneficial and harmful use of such technology, saying that "it would be surprising if many hours per day of screen activity did not influence this neuroplasticity".<ref name="Bell h3064">{{Cite journal|title=The debate over digital technology and young people|url=http://www.bmj.com/content/351/bmj.h3064|journal=The BMJ|date=12 August 2015|issn=1756-1833|pmid=26268481|article-number=h3064|volume=351|doi=10.1136/bmj.h3064|first1=Vaughan|last1=Bell|first2=Dorothy V.M.|last2=Bishop|first3=Andrew K.|last3=Przybylski|s2cid=20209855|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Honours==
As of 2016, Greenfield has 32 honorary degrees;<ref>{{cite news |title=‘Rock star’ scientist slammed |date=13 August 2015 |work=[[The Australian]] |access-date=5 April 2016 |url-access=subscription |url=https://www.theaustralian.com.au/nation/health-science/colleagues-slam-rockstar-scientist-over-autisminternet-campaign/news-story/fdbfd4558f2230ff20771bbe3b043ee5}}</ref> has received awards including the [[Royal Society]]'s [[Michael Faraday Prize]]. She has been elected to an Honorary Fellowship of the [[Royal College of Physicians]]<ref name="Rigb.org">{{cite web|url=http://www.rigb.org/contentControl?action=displayContent&id=00000001145|title=Bio on the Royal Institution website|publisher=Rigb.org|access-date=2 December 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120211203226/http://www.rigb.org/contentControl?action=displayContent&id=00000001145|archive-date=11 February 2012}}</ref> and the London [[Science Museum, London|Science Museum]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sciencemuseum.org.uk/about_us/fellows.aspx|title=Fellows – About us|publisher=Science Museum|date=2 September 2011|access-date=8 July 2013|archive-date=2 July 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130702205334/http://www.sciencemuseum.org.uk/about_us/fellows.aspx}}</ref>

In 2006 she was made an Honorary Fellow of the [[British Science Association]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.britishscienceassociation.org/about-british-science-association/our-organisation/honorary-fellows/current-honorary-fellows|title=Current Honorary Fellows|publisher=British Science Association|access-date=17 June 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140725022608/http://www.britishscienceassociation.org/about-british-science-association/our-organisation/honorary-fellows/current-honorary-fellows|archive-date=25 July 2014}}</ref> and was the Honorary Australian of the Year.<ref>{{Citation|chapter=Greenfield, Baroness, (Susan Adele Greenfield) (born 1 Oct. 1950)|date=2007-12-01|chapter-url=http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/10.1093/ww/9780199540884.001.0001/ww-9780199540884-e-18067|title=Who's Who|publisher=Oxford University Press|language=en|doi=10.1093/ww/9780199540884.013.u18067|isbn=978-0-19-954088-4 |access-date=2019-12-07|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref>

In [[2000 New Year Honours|January 2000]], Greenfield received a [[Commander of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire|CBE]]<ref>{{London Gazette|issue=55710|date=31 December 1999|page=9 |supp=y}}</ref> for her contribution to the public understanding of science.<ref name="baroness"/> Later that year, she was named Woman of the Year<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/theobserver/2000/dec/31/features.review67|title=Your Woman of the Year|last=Anthony|first=Andrew|date=2000-12-31|work=The Observer|access-date=2019-12-07|language=en-GB|issn=0029-7712}}</ref> by ''[[The Observer]]''. In 2001, she became a [[Life peer|Life Peer]] under the [[House of Lords Appointments Commission]] system,<ref name="theguardian.com">{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2001/apr/27/uk.Whitehall|title=The people's peers: seven knights, a lord's wife and three professors|website=[[TheGuardian.com]] |date=27 April 2001 |access-date=13 August 2015 |last1=Perkins |first1=Anne }}</ref> as Baroness Greenfield, of [[Otmoor|Ot Moor]], [[Oxfordshire]].<ref name="baroness"/><ref>{{London Gazette|issue=56252|date=21 June 2001|page=7343}}</ref> Like the other people's peers she was self-nominated.<ref name="theguardian.com"/>

In 2003, she was appointed a Knight of the [[Legion of Honour]] by the [[Government of France|French Government]].<ref name="Rigb.org"/> In 2010 she was awarded the Australian Society for Medical Research Medal.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.asmr.org.au/MRW.html|title=MRW|website=asmr.org.au|publisher=Australian Society for Medical Research|access-date=17 June 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130509105214/http://www.asmr.org.au/MRW.html|archive-date=9 May 2013}}</ref> She received the British Inspiration award for Science and Technology in 2010.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://britishinspirationawards.co.uk/awards/2010/#http://britishinspirationawards.co.uk/portfolio/baroness-susan-adele-greenfield|title=2010 Awards|publisher=British Inspiration Awards|access-date=17 June 2013}}</ref>

==Patronage==
She is a patron of [[Alzheimer's Research UK]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.alzheimersresearchuk.org/patrons/|title=Patrons|publisher=Alzheimer's Research UK|access-date=12 August 2014|archive-date=23 September 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130923190942/http://www.alzheimersresearchuk.org/patrons/}}</ref> and of [[Dignity in Dying]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Brian Pretty and Zoe Wanamaker among new patrons for Dignity in Dying (Jan 23) – Dignity in Dying|work=Dignity in Dying |date=23 January 2006 |url=http://www.dignityindying.org.uk/press-release/brian-pretty-and-zoe-wanamaker-among-new-patrons-for-dignity-in-dying-jan-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160424131821/http://www.dignityindying.org.uk/press-release/brian-pretty-and-zoe-wanamaker-among-new-patrons-for-dignity-in-dying-jan-23/|archive-date=24 April 2016|access-date=17 September 2015}}</ref> She is a founder and trustee of the charity Science for Humanity, a network of scientists, researchers and technologists that collaborates with not-for-profit organisations to create practical solutions to the everyday problems of developing communities.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Global Risk Register – About Science for Humanity|url=https://www.globalriskregister.org/about-us/about-science-for-humanity.html|website=globalriskregister.org|access-date=17 September 2015|archive-date=4 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304053543/https://www.globalriskregister.org/about-us/about-science-for-humanity.html}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Greenfield was married to the [[University of Oxford]] professor [[Peter Atkins]] from 1991 until their divorce in 2005.<ref name="ind08">{{cite news|first=Cole|last=Moreton|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/science/susan-greenfield-the-girl-with-all-the-brains-825916.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220525/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/science/susan-greenfield-the-girl-with-all-the-brains-825916.html |archive-date=25 May 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=Susan Greenfield: The girl with all the brains|newspaper=The Independent on Sunday|date=11 May 2008|location=London, UK|access-date=16 April 2016}}</ref>
